newsitem.title: THAILAND: Power-broker defence chief aims to be new Thai PM.
newsitem.headline: Power-broker defence chief aims to be new Thai PM.

text.p: Thai Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said on Thursday he had been a behind-the-scenes power-broker for too long and now wanted to become prime minister after the November 17 general election.
Chavalit, who claimed he was behind former prime minister General Prem Tinsulananda's ascendancy to the premiership in 1980, said he had "waited long enough".
"I have given chances (to be prime minister) to somebody else for the last 35 years already. This country needs repair, it needs leadership," he told Reuters in an interview.

The former army chief, who heads the New Aspiration Party (NAP) and is seen as a front-runner for the premiership, also said he was instrumental in enabling ex-diplomat General Chatichai Choonhavan become prime minister in 1988.
He said Thailand, currently beset by major economic woes such as a widening current account deficit and loss of investor confidence, needed strong leadership and he was prepared to offer that.
"We have no more time. Time is running short and we are already so far behind," he said.

After 14 months under the administration of the six-member coalition government of outgoing premier Banharn Silpa-archa, Thailand faces a slowing economy, sagging exports, a stock market that is at three-year-lows and high interest rates.

Chavalit, whose NAP was a senior coalition partner in the outgoing coalition, appeared set to assume the premiership from Banharn in late September after he forced Banharn to publicly declare he would resign.
But Banharn turned the tables on Chavalit at the last minute and, despite protests from coalition partners, dissolved parliament and set fresh polls in November.
Political analysts called it vintage Chavalit -- so close but yet so far from the top job.

Chavalit said this time he was 100 percent confident of making it to the premiership because he expected his NAP, which won 57 seats in the last polls, to take more than 100 seats in the election for the 393-seat parliament.
"We expect to win at least 100 plus seats in this election ...To answer your question, I am 100 percent sure (of becoming premier)," he said, when asked of his election chances.
Thailand has been ruled by coalition governments since the parliamentary system was introduced in 1932.

Chavalit pledged that the Thai military, which has launched 17 coups or coup attempts since 1932, would remain out of politics. "I can guarantee you the military won't come in (to politics) anymore," he said.

The NAP recently benefited heavily from a series of defections by members of parliament from Banharn's Chart Thai party and other smaller parties. Some opposition parties accused the cash-rich NAP of enticing them with money, but Chavalit said this was untrue.

In an interview, former premier and leader of the opposition Chart Pattana party, Chatichai Choonhavan, said: "That we have money politics and vote buying is a shame. This is going to be the last election with old style politics because after this one there will be a new constitution."
Chart Pattana, with 53 seats now, expected to win up to 70 seats, said Chatichai, who could be the vital link in the formation of any new coalition after the polls.
